Final Report on Observations, Conclusions, and Results of Portulaca Oleracea
Purslane Gang: Reeva Khan, Ethan Agustin-Calloway, Joe Nylasi, Avery Leftman, Camila
Quino, Elijah Woods, Willa Tansey, and Melana Shiring
Heritage High School
17244
Highschool

2
Title and Team #
Our team is the Purslane Gang, 17244, and our group is attempting to plant the moon.
Background
Purslane (Portulaca oleracea) is a durable plant that needs water roughly every 3 weeks,
however due to the circumstances the Purslane Gang has decided to grow them indoors to
produce spring/summer conditions (Guide, n.d.). Purslane is edible and can be ready to eat in
around 6-8 weeks (Guide n.d.). The goal for this project is to see how well purslane would be
able to grow in lunar regolith mixed with soil in different ratios to produce an edible plant. While
plants can grow in lunar regolith, the development and lifespan can be fragile (Keeter 2022).
Since this succulent is durable and low maintenance, it is a suitable plant to try growing on lunar
regolith.
The point of growing plants/crops in lunar regolith is the future benefits it can have.
Learning how to grow edible plants in lunar regolith opens up possibilities to growing plant life
on the moon, and that further opens up ideas of long-term space travel and habitation. All of this
must begin with trying on lunar regolith here on earth with earthly conditions. Lunar regolith is a
very grainy and sand-like substance. Lunar regolith, despite sharing analogous names with
earth’s soil, has little to no agricultural component in it because of it being largely composed of
lunar-exclusive minerals and glass forged by solar winds and meteoroid interactions (Noble p.
1-2). The reason why it is so difficult to grow plants in regolith is the lack of nutrients. Purslane
was chosen because of its ability to do well in harsh conditions and its ability to do well in more
compact soils.

3
Experiment Design
Pots were set 5x4, each column - of 5 pots - being one type of lunar regolith to soil ratio.
The control group was pure Earth soil, and the rest of the groups were 50:50, 60:40, and 70:30
(Lunar regolith : Earth soil). Each pot held about 350 mL of soil and 3 purslane seeds in each of
the 20 pots. The measurement of lunar regolith and earth soil was first calculated by percentages.
For example:
60% 𝑙𝑢𝑛𝑎𝑟 𝑟𝑒𝑔𝑜𝑙𝑖𝑡ℎ
100% 𝑤ℎ𝑜𝑙𝑒
= 𝑥 𝑚𝐿 𝑙𝑢𝑛𝑎𝑟 𝑟𝑒𝑔𝑜𝑙𝑖𝑡ℎ
350 𝑚𝐿 𝑤ℎ𝑜𝑙𝑒
→210 𝑚𝐿 = 𝑥
Hence, the 50:50 group was comprised of 175 mL lunar regolith and 175 mL earth soil, the
60:40 was 210 mL lunar regolith and 140 mL earth soil, the 70:30 was 245 mL lunar regolith and
105 mL earth soil, and the 0:100 group was 350 mL earth soil. The earth soil and lunar regolith
was tightly packed and evenly mixed with each other before placement in the pots. The pots
were about 4 inches tall, wide, and long. Seeds were planted ¼ inches deep and given a little bit
of distance between each.
Fertilizer would only be added in late February to early March, where the initial planned
fertilizer was a slow-release 10-10-10 fertilizer, but later on when it came time for
implementation, it was amended to use a liquid Miracle Grow fertilizer that would be put in the
water rather than directly applied to the soil. Initially, 55 mL of fertilizer was added to the water
every other data collection day. Later on in the experiment, fertilizer was changed from 55 mL to
50 mL to adjust with the water system.
For watering, we used regular tap water to fill up a beaker of 1000 mL every time data
collection occurred, and we recorded how much water was used or refilled. The watering was not
administered by hand, but rather by a drip irrigation system that used tubes to pour a specified
amount of water into each pot at a set time. The drip irrigation system sourced this water from

4
the 1000 mL beaker. This watering system measured the amount of water given by how long it
watered the plants.
In planning the experiment, research found that purslanes only needed to be watered
118.294 mL (or .5 cups) every 3 weeks of distilled water, but this was soon changed in
adaptation to be 10 mL to each plant of regular tap water every day. In total, it was around 200
mL of regular water being given everyday, however the watering system used did not measure
water given by how much water, instead going by how long the purslanes were watered. For the
majority of February and the first days of March, the plants were watered about 8 seconds a day
at 1:20 p.m. This too would be amended once the decline in purslanes’ health was noticed, and it
was changed to be 15 seconds of water every day (which was about 375 mL). This remained
until the end of the growing period.
Hypotheses
What conditions of lunar regolith and earth soil can most efficiently allow purslane seeds
to grow to an edible state of quality? Upon potting plants, it will be found that a composition of
60% lunar regolith,40% earth soil, along with (about) 55 mL of fertilizer, will be the most
suitable for purslane to grow to a point of being edible.
Independent Variables
The independent variable in this case is the lunar regolith, as we change the ratio of lunar
regolith to earth soil in each group.
Dependent Variables
By using the independent variable, the dependent variables are the plants’ growth and
life. For example, number of sprouts, sprout height, how long each one lived, and their overall
appearance.

5
Measurements & Procedures
The data was collected every 2-4 days on a school schedule, from around 3:50 - 4:10 pm
We measured sprout height, evaluated plant’s appearance and condition, and soil’s condition.
Gloves were used when handling the purslanes, but were discarded when checking the dampness
of soil.
Data collection primarily consisted of recording 3 aspects: how much water was given
administered to the plants, sprout height, and # of sprouts. The first was done by checking how
many mL of water were left every data collection day (about every other day) and subtracting
that from 1000. Using this, we could calculate how much water was being given to each plant
individually. Another method was to take a small beaker or graduated cylinder, place one of the
drip irrigation system tubes in it, press the button to water the plants, measure how much water
was served to a singular plant, and estimate how much water all the plants consumed. Counting
the number of sprouts was recorded onto a digital sheet and a paper. Measuring spout height was
done by taking a ruler and counting each sprout in each group’s individual height in centimeters,
to which this data would be recorded on a digital sheet and paper. If a sprout was drooping over a
little, we would use a thin, straight object (like a pencil or pen) and hold it up to measure it. If the
plant was completely collapsed on the soil, it would be measured at a height of 0 cm.
Everytime data was collected, the watering system would be checked; how much water
was being given or if there were any errors in the tubes. Someone would also remove their
gloves and gently feel or touch the soil of one pot from each group to check the dampness levels
in the soil for each group. Occasionally, we would use gloves and gently feel the stems of some
purslanes to see how thin, thick, fragile, or firm they were. All of these were done with extreme
care so as not to move anything out of place, uproot, or harm the purslanes.

6
Controls
Out of our 4 total groups, one of them served as our control group with a 0:100 ratio of
lunar regolith to earth soil percentages. This group was grown and watched in the same manner
as the other groups, but the only isolating factor (and point of comparison) was these plants’ lack
of any lunar regolith in them.
Results
From the span of February 5 to March 22, there were 38 seeds that managed to sprout out
of the 60, however by the final days they had all died. The peak of growth recorded was on
February 16, when all 38 sprouts
had appeared and the average
sprout height was around .81 cm.
From there, the plants grew until
the point of March 11, when all
had died off. The amount of
seedlings decreased at a rate of
3.61 seeds per two days, but this
graph does not fully account for the dying/dead seedlings; only for existing sprouts. Out of all of
them, the 50:50 group
and the 60:40 remained
the most persistent, and
the 50:50 group held out
quite consistently with
little change over the

7
days. However, only the amount of seeds cannot suffice for results because the actual conditions
of the plants often fluctuated no matter how many seeds were alive. In terms of growth of
purslane, the sprouts steadily grew to a maximum height of 5.2 cm inches by March 7th. On
March 7th, the plants reached their highest average of about 2.69 cm tall. Despite the 60:40
group’s attrition of sprouts, this group reached the tallest height out of all of them while the
50:50 trailed behind closely. On the other hand, between February 29th and March 4th, the
control group (0:100) and 50:50 group had completely died off. Accounting for all of them, the
average height of purslane decreased at a rate of -3.17 cm per two days. Although, the disparity
of two groups increasing in height with two groups that remain at 0 may have altered the average
increase of height in the graph. Ignoring the groups that died off, the average would instead have
been increasing.
On another note, the physical appearance of the purslane aligned with the data. In the first
week to mid second week (and majority of March), the purslanes had pinkish-purple stems and
1-2 leaves or 3 at most. At the beginning of the decline in the data, between February 29th and
March 4th, the purslanes began to droop. Instead of standing tall like most healthy purslanes,
they bent over and some even collapsed. In the final days of data collection (near March 11th to
March 13th), some sprouts had not died but remained collapsed on the soil, and in order to
account for them, they were still recorded but as having a height of 0 cm. On March 13th, there
may have been 6 seeds, however none could stand. Thus, they were all listed as having a height
of 0 cm. For the majority of March, the stems of purslanes would slowly turn thin and white
before failing to sustain their weight. Their leaves became fragile along with the stems, as they
were malleable and thinning. Not to mention, the smell of the purslane increasingly became

8
stronger and less pleasant near the final days. Ultimately, after March 13th, all purslane plants
had completely died.
Discussion & Conclusions
Based on these results, the decline in purslane health and their eventual death is largely
attributed to two factors: lack of proper care and the purslanes’ incompatibility with lunar
regolith. The biggest issue with care for purslane was our oversight in experiment design. The
experiment outline was heavily centered around watering, leading to other large factors like
temperature, lighting, and pH being ignored. Throughout the experiment, the primary factor
being recorded, aside from the purslanes themselves, was the water: how much was being given,
the impact of water, the adjustments for water, what kind of water, and so on. When discussing
the causes of purslane dying, it was entirely imputed onto the watering system.
The watering system initially was set to be watering for 25 seconds a day, however errors
were made in adjusting the watering system. We changed the drip irrigation system to water 8
seconds a day when we thought it was watering too much due to the constantly damp soil, and
for the rest of the growing period until mid March, we attempted to change the amount of time
watering from 8 to 10 to 15 to 16, and then to 20. Soon, we realized that the watering time had
not changed, and we had made unfounded assumptions regarding the lack of purslane life. Once
we discovered this, we made the final watering adjustment to 15 seconds of watering time.
Understanding this, the data leads us to believe that the watering did hold a larger hand over the
purslanes’ health in the beginning, but near the middle of the growing period it shrunk in
importance (while we perceived it to grow). This is because of how the soil very clearly showed
effects of the watering; too dry or too moist. When it was kept at 8 and 15 seconds of watering
time later on, the soil no longer showed these signs while at decent conditions.

9
Despite the water holding a decent portion of cause for the purslanes’ decline, the
unregulated temperature, pH, fertilizer, and lighting were also affecting the purslane. Throughout
the experiment, not much mind was paid to the temperature of the purslanes despite their optimal
temperatures for growth being 68℉- 100.4℉(or 20℃- 38℃). Purslanes are better in warmer
temperatures, but being grown in a school classroom in near room temperatures without change
may have also been the cause for stunted growth. A classroom with small, electricity based lights
cannot compare to the sunlight and its colors either; which is another condition critical for
purslanes. Not to mention, the pH went entirely unrecorded the entire experiment. This factor
may have had smaller impacts, but is still important due to the lunar regolith having a much more
alkaline pH (with less acidity due to its lack of nutrients and elements). If it was measured, it
could have been better regulated and accounted for in terms of the purslanes’ demise.
Another important possibility to the purslanes’ death could be the purslanes’
incompatibility with lunar regolith. Since lunar regolith contains little to no nutrients, the only
nutrients it would’ve received would be through the soil and fertilizer. When analyzing the
growth of purslane, despite the dwindling number of seeds over the days, the living ones grew
exponentially tall; perhaps not to an ideal state or even edible one, but the fact that there was a
big jump between March 4th and March 7th where the sole plant of the 60:40 group reached the
maximum height of 5.2 cm tall, even in their devolving conditions, suggests positive plant
growth. During this time, this 60:40 plant had a purple stem and 2 leaves, and appeared to almost
be healthy. The anomaly-like seed growing perfectly fine despite a factor that had killed almost
all of the seeds suggests an inconsistency, and this inconsistency implies individual deaths of the
purslanes rather than death as a group from a large ailment. Referring to Table 1 on the number
of sprouts in each group, the decline in seeds is different across each group. Every group

10
decreased at separate times and separate rates. While the 70:30 group and the control group had
both died off by March 4th, the two decreased at entirely different rates. The 70:30 group
decreased steeply, even coming back February 29th, while the control group more so faded. The
60:40 fluctuated while the 50:50 remained consistent. Disregarding the control group, these
numbers do not lean towards a large, overall ailment, but individual deaths. This sounds more
like the plants succumbing to their inability to grow in lunar regolith at their own paces. While
the lack of care definitely played a role, seeing as the control group should have theoretically
held the best results died off first, the simple disparity between the nutrients and conditions lunar
regolith can provide and the nutrients and conditions a plant needs could have played a large role
in this as well.
The results we produced out of this experiment were much more diverse and expansive
than we had expected. In our hypothesis, we predicted that the 60:40 group would effectively
grow to a state of being edible. In our results, while the 60:40 grew to be the highest, their
numbers dwindled low to the point of being less than the control group that died off first and the
70:30 group. None of the plants grew to a point of being edible, but the results did not entirely
throw away the idea of purslane in lunar regolith. Yes, the 60:40 group seemingly flourished
more than the other seeds, but the attrition of 60:40 seeds cannot be ignored either. While these
results do not support our hypothesis, they instead show potential for a better designed
experiment that could yield much more accurate and higher quality results.
If there was another chance to redo the experiment, the biggest thing that would be
focused on would be fixing the watering system so that we properly record and understand the
effects of water in the plants. However, in this experiment we focused too much on watering and
neglected other handles of care in the process. Thus, the second thing that would be focused on

11
would be paying more attention and measuring surrounding temperatures, pH, and making sure
the lights above were not too bright or too dim. A large part of this issue was due to the
miscalculation of their part in purslane growth. The next experiment we do will definitely go
over any and all factors necessary. The final thing we would change is our methods of data
collection, as the number of sprouts and height of sprouts cannot fully account for the qualitative
data as well.
